Disclosed is a method for preparing a liquid formulation that can form a polymer electrolyte membrane with reduced cracking or rupture during drying. Also disclosed is a method for preparing a coating liquid for catalyst-layer formation that can produce a catalyst layer resistant to damage during drying, as well as a method for manufacturing a membrane/electrode assembly in which either the catalyst layer or the polymer electrolyte membrane is less likely to break during drying.

The method for producing the liquid formulation includes maintaining a fluorinated polymer containing —SO₂F groups at a temperature of 110 to 130°C for 45 minutes or longer; then lowering the temperature of the fluorinated polymer containing —SO₂F groups to below 110°C; subsequently converting the —SO₂F groups in the cooled fluorinated polymer into ion-exchange groups to obtain a fluorinated polymer bearing ion-exchange groups; and finally combining that ion-exchange-group-containing fluorinated polymer with a liquid medium.

The text describes a set of production processes for liquid compositions, catalyst layer-forming coating liquids, and membrane/electrode assemblies that are designed to suppress breakage during drying. These processes are particularly useful in the manufacture of polymer electrolyte membranes and related electrochemical components, where cracking or breakage during solvent removal can reduce product quality and performance.

The liquid composition is intended for forming a polymer electrolyte membrane that is less prone to drying-related breakage. To achieve this, the process begins with a fluorinated polymer containing —SO₂F groups. This fluorinated polymer is subjected to a heat-holding treatment in which it is maintained at a temperature of 110 to 130° C. for at least 45 minutes. This controlled heating step is important for improving the properties of the polymer before it is converted into its ion-conductive form.

After the heat treatment, the fluorinated polymer is cooled to a temperature below 110° C. before any further chemical conversion is carried out. Once cooled, the —SO₂F groups in the fluorinated polymer are converted into ion exchange groups. This conversion produces a fluorinated polymer suitable for use as a polymer electrolyte material.

The resulting fluorinated polymer is then mixed with a liquid medium to prepare the liquid composition. This composition can be used to form a polymer electrolyte membrane with improved resistance to breakage during drying. In addition, the same liquid composition may be used in the preparation of catalyst layer-forming coating liquids and membrane/electrode assemblies, thereby contributing to the production of durable electrochemical devices with fewer defects caused by drying stresses.
outputs.L4:
A process is provided for producing liquid compositions, catalyst-layer coating liquids, and membrane/electrode assemblies that exhibit reduced cracking and breakage during drying. The process uses a fluorinated polymer having sulfonyl fluoride groups represented by —SO₂F. This polymer is first subjected to a heat treatment under controlled conditions, and is then cooled. After cooling, the —SO₂F groups in the fluorinated polymer are converted into ion-exchange groups, such as sulfonic acid groups or salt-form sulfonate groups. The resulting ion-exchange fluorinated polymer is then mixed with a liquid medium to obtain a liquid composition.

The liquid composition produced by this method is useful as a material for forming polymer electrolyte membranes and catalyst layers. Because the fluorinated polymer is heat-treated before conversion of the sulfonyl fluoride groups, the resulting composition has improved behavior during film formation and drying. In particular, when the liquid composition is applied to a substrate and dried, breakage, cracking, and other defects caused by drying stress are effectively suppressed.

The process can also be used to prepare catalyst-layer coating liquids. In this case, the liquid composition containing the ion-exchange fluorinated polymer is combined with catalyst particles, such as noble-metal-supported carbon particles, and optionally with additional solvent or additives. The resulting catalyst-layer coating liquid can be applied to a gas diffusion layer, a polymer electrolyte membrane, or another suitable substrate to form a catalyst layer. Since drying-related cracking is reduced, the catalyst layer can be formed more uniformly and with improved mechanical integrity.

A membrane/electrode assembly can be produced by using the polymer electrolyte membrane and/or catalyst layer obtained from the liquid composition or catalyst-layer coating liquid. For example, catalyst layers may be formed on both sides of a polymer electrolyte membrane to produce an assembly suitable for use in a fuel cell. The reduced occurrence of cracks and breaks during drying contributes to improved durability, reliability, and production yield of the membrane/electrode assembly.

Accordingly, the described process provides a practical method for manufacturing fluorinated-polymer-based liquid compositions and related electrochemical components. By combining heat treatment, cooling, conversion of —SO₂F groups into ion-exchange groups, and dispersion or dissolution in a liquid medium, the process enables the formation of membranes and catalyst layers that are less susceptible to drying defects and are therefore well suited for high-performance membrane/electrode assemblies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the following fuel cell membrane invention in patent-style language: suppressing breakage during drying by heat-treating a fluorinated polymer having sulfonyl fluoride groups before converting them to ion exchange groups.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention relates to a process for producing a fluorinated ion-exchange membrane suitable for use as a fuel cell electrolyte membrane. The process comprises heat-treating a fluorinated polymer membrane or film containing sulfonyl fluoride groups prior to conversion of said sulfonyl fluoride groups into ion-exchange groups, such as sulfonic acid groups or salts thereof.

By subjecting the precursor polymer having sulfonyl fluoride groups to a predetermined heat treatment before hydrolysis or acidification, internal stress and structural instability of the membrane are reduced. As a result, when the membrane is subsequently converted to the ion-exchange form and dried, occurrence of cracking, tearing, rupture, or other breakage is suppressed.

The fluorinated polymer is preferably a perfluorinated polymer containing repeating units derived from a fluorinated olefin and a fluorinated monomer having a sulfonyl fluoride group. After heat treatment, the sulfonyl fluoride groups are converted into ion-exchange groups by hydrolysis and, if necessary, acid treatment, thereby obtaining a fluorinated ion-exchange membrane having improved drying durability.

Accordingly, the invention provides a method for manufacturing a fuel cell membrane which exhibits reduced breakage during drying while maintaining desirable proton conductivity, chemical resistance, and mechanical properties required for fuel cell operation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an English patent claim/abstract describing a process for producing a polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition and catalyst layer coating liquid, where a fluorinated polymer is held at 110 to 130°C for at least 45 minutes, cooled below 110°C, converted from —SO2F groups to ion exchange groups, then dispersed in a liquid medium.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

A process is provided for producing a polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition and a catalyst layer coating liquid. The process comprises heat-treating a fluorinated polymer having —SO₂F groups at a temperature of 110 to 130°C for at least 45 minutes, cooling the heat-treated fluorinated polymer to a temperature below 110°C, converting at least a portion of the —SO₂F groups of the cooled fluorinated polymer into ion exchange groups, and dispersing the resulting ion exchange group-containing fluorinated polymer in a liquid medium to obtain a polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition. A catalyst layer coating liquid is further produced by mixing the liquid composition with a catalyst and, optionally, an electrically conductive carrier and/or an additional solvent. The process provides a stable liquid composition suitable for forming a polymer electrolyte membrane or an electrode catalyst layer for an electrochemical device.

**Claim**

1. A process for producing a polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition, the process comprising:  
   holding a fluorinated polymer comprising —SO₂F groups at a temperature of 110 to 130°C for a period of at least 45 minutes;  
   cooling the fluorinated polymer after said holding to a temperature below 110°C;  
   converting at least a portion of the —SO₂F groups of the cooled fluorinated polymer into ion exchange groups; and  
   dispersing the fluorinated polymer having the ion exchange groups in a liquid medium to obtain the polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition.

2. The process according to claim 1, wherein the ion exchange groups comprise sulfonic acid groups or salts thereof.

3. The process according to claim 1, wherein converting the —SO₂F groups comprises hydrolysis followed by acid treatment.

4. The process according to claim 1, wherein the liquid medium comprises water, an alcohol, or a mixed solvent containing water and an alcohol.

5. The process according to claim 1, wherein the fluorinated polymer is a perfluorinated polymer comprising units derived from a fluorinated olefin and units having a sulfonyl fluoride group-containing side chain.

6. A process for producing a catalyst layer coating liquid, comprising producing the polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition by the process according to claim 1, and mixing the polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition with a catalyst.

7. The process according to claim 6, wherein the catalyst comprises platinum or a platinum alloy supported on carbon.

8. A polymer electrolyte membrane-forming liquid composition produced by the process according to claim 1.

9. A catalyst layer coating liquid produced by the process according to claim 6.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical “problem and solution” section for a patent on membrane/electrode assembly production that prevents cracking or breakage during drying of catalyst layers or polymer electrolyte membranes.
counterfactuals.output:
## Problem

In the production of membrane/electrode assemblies for electrochemical devices, such as polymer electrolyte fuel cells, water electrolyzers, electrochemical hydrogen pumps, and related cells, catalyst layers and polymer electrolyte membranes are commonly formed from coating liquids containing ionomer, catalyst particles, conductive carbon, solvents, water, and/or polymer electrolyte components. After application onto a substrate, transfer film, gas diffusion layer, or electrolyte membrane, the coated layer is dried to remove volatile components.

During drying, however, the coating layer undergoes volumetric shrinkage as solvent evaporates and as the polymer electrolyte or ionomer consolidates. Because the wet coating is typically constrained by adhesion to an underlying substrate or by nonuniform solvent removal through the thickness of the layer, tensile stress develops within the drying layer. If the stress exceeds the cohesive strength of the wet or partially dried layer, cracks, fissures, pinholes, delamination, curling, or fracture may occur.

This problem is particularly significant where:

1. the catalyst layer has a high solids content or high catalyst loading;  
2. the layer includes brittle or highly filled catalyst/carbon/ionomer structures;  
3. the polymer electrolyte membrane is thin and mechanically weak in the swollen state;  
4. drying is performed rapidly at elevated temperature or low humidity;  
5. a coated layer is dried while fixed at its edges or adhered to a dimensionally stable carrier; or  
6. the layer experiences nonuniform drying between its surface and its interior.

Cracking or breakage of the catalyst layer or electrolyte membrane causes local discontinuities in proton-conductive pathways, catalyst utilization loss, increased gas crossover, electrical shorting, reduced interfacial adhesion, nonuniform current density, and degraded durability. In severe cases, the membrane/electrode assembly cannot be laminated or incorporated into a cell stack. Even when cracks are microscopic, they may expand during hot pressing, hydration/dehydration cycling, cell start-up and shut-down, or pressure cycling, resulting in reduced power output and shortened service life.

Conventional approaches to this problem include lowering drying temperature, increasing drying time, reducing coating thickness, or increasing binder content. However, these approaches reduce productivity, restrict catalyst loading, increase material cost, or impair electrochemical performance by increasing mass transport resistance or lowering porosity. Accordingly, there is a need for a membrane/electrode assembly production method that suppresses cracking, fracture, and delamination during drying while maintaining high productivity and desirable electrochemical properties.

## Solution

The present technology provides a method for producing a membrane/electrode assembly in which cracking or breakage during drying is suppressed by controlling stress generation and stress relaxation in a catalyst layer and/or polymer electrolyte membrane while volatile components are removed. In one embodiment, the method includes forming a wet coating layer containing an electrode catalyst and an ion-conductive polymer, and drying the wet coating layer under conditions selected such that shrinkage stress generated in the layer does not exceed a fracture threshold of the layer during at least an initial drying stage.

In one aspect, the method comprises:

1. preparing a coating composition containing a catalyst component, an ionomer or polymer electrolyte, and a solvent system;  
2. applying the coating composition onto a support, transfer substrate, gas diffusion medium, or polymer electrolyte membrane to form a wet catalyst layer;  
3. subjecting the wet catalyst layer to a first drying step under a controlled atmosphere having a prescribed humidity, solvent vapor concentration, temperature, and/or gas flow rate so as to remove solvent gradually from a surface portion of the wet layer;  
4. subjecting the partially dried layer to a stress-relaxation step in which the layer is maintained at a temperature and humidity at which polymer chains or ionomer domains remain deformable; and  
5. completing drying in a second drying step at a higher drying rate or higher temperature after the layer has acquired sufficient cohesive strength to resist cracking.

By dividing drying into a plurality of stages, the coating layer is not exposed to abrupt surface skin formation or steep solvent concentration gradients. Internal stress is therefore reduced, and any shrinkage that occurs during solvent removal can be accommodated by viscous flow, polymer relaxation, or controlled dimensional change of the layer.

In another aspect, the support or carrier on which the catalyst layer or membrane is formed is configured to permit shrinkage of the drying layer. For example, the wet layer may be supported on a releasable, stretchable, low-adhesion, or dimensionally compliant substrate. The substrate may include a fluororesin film, silicone-treated film, elastomeric film, porous support, or release-coated carrier having an adhesion force selected to hold the wet layer during coating while allowing in-plane shrinkage during drying. By reducing mechanical constraint between the layer and the carrier, tensile stress in the drying layer is reduced.

In a further aspect, the drying step is performed while maintaining the wet layer in a humidified environment. Relative humidity may be controlled, for example, within a range that prevents premature solidification of an ionomer-rich surface region. The controlled humidity may be decreased stepwise or continuously during drying. This suppresses formation of a dense surface skin that would otherwise trap solvent inside the layer and generate nonuniform shrinkage.

In another embodiment, solvent removal is controlled by using a solvent system containing at least two solvents having different vapor pressures. A relatively volatile solvent may be removed first to increase viscosity and prevent flow defects, while a less volatile solvent remains temporarily in the layer to provide plasticization and stress relaxation. Subsequent removal of the less volatile solvent is performed after the layer has developed a mechanically continuous structure. The solvent composition, drying temperature, and vapor concentration are selected to balance drying productivity with crack prevention.

In yet another aspect, the catalyst layer or membrane is dried while being subjected to a mechanical stress-control operation. The operation may include supporting the layer without edge fixation, applying low tension to prevent wrinkling while avoiding excessive restraint, intermittently relaxing web tension, or drying the layer on a curved or moving support that reduces differential shrinkage. Where the layer is produced in a roll-to-roll process, web tension may be controlled in coordination with solvent content so that the wet layer is not stretched or constrained beyond a predetermined strain limit.

In one embodiment, a polymer electrolyte membrane is produced or handled in a hydrated or solvent-swollen state and is dried using a staged temperature/humidity profile. The membrane may be temporarily reinforced by a porous support, removable carrier, mesh, sacrificial film, or edge support during coating and drying. The support prevents tearing or breakage of the thin membrane while permitting controlled dimensional change. After drying or after lamination with catalyst layers, the support may be removed or retained as a reinforcing member.

In another embodiment, the catalyst layer includes a stress-relief component in an amount sufficient to improve crack resistance without substantially impairing electrochemical performance. The stress-relief component may include an ionomer of adjusted equivalent weight, a flexible polymer, a high-boiling plasticizing solvent, a pore-forming agent, short fibers, nanofibers, fibrillated polymer, or a particulate additive that improves toughness of the partially dried layer. The component may be removed during subsequent heat treatment or retained in the electrode structure.

In a preferred implementation, a wet catalyst layer is dried by a first drying zone maintained at a relatively low temperature and controlled humidity to reduce solvent concentration gradients, followed by an intermediate hold zone that allows stress relaxation, followed by a final drying zone at a higher temperature to remove residual solvent. The drying conditions may be selected based on at least one measured or estimated parameter, such as residual solvent content, coating surface temperature, layer shrinkage rate, elastic modulus, tensile stress, web tension, or crack initiation threshold. Feedback control may be used to adjust drying gas temperature, humidity, flow velocity, infrared heating intensity, or residence time.

The solution is applicable to catalyst-coated membranes, catalyst-coated gas diffusion layers, decal transfer films, reinforced electrolyte membranes, unsupported electrolyte membranes, and roll-to-roll or batch production processes. By controlling drying-induced stress through staged drying, humidity regulation, solvent-vapor management, compliant support, tension control, and/or material modification, the production method prevents cracking, breakage, and delamination while enabling high catalyst loading, thin membrane formation, improved yield, and stable electrochemical performance.
